newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK investors welcome $20 bln BT deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK investors welcome $20 bln BT deal.

text.p: Shares in British Telecom Plc forged ahead in heavy trading on Monday as investors welcomed the group's planned $20 billion merger with MCI Communications of the United States.

BT said it was optimistic that the European Commission would clear the largest cross-border takeover deal in history, a merger that will create one of the largest groups in the rapidly expanding global telecommunications sector.
Britain's Oftel watchdog body said it was studying the details of the merger and it was too early to pass judgement.
British, European and U.S. regulators will subject the deal to close scrutiny amid strong opposition to it from rivals including American long-distance market leader AT&T Corp.
BT chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield has said it could take a year to clear all the regulatory hurdles.
BT shares powered 32 1/2 higher to 383 1/2p at 1215 GMT -- around two billion pounds ($3.3 billion) to the company's market value in huge trading volume of over 40 million shares.

Despite the large cost of the deal to BT -- it will be the biggest-ever acquisition by a British firm -- the merger is seen as having a compelling industrial logic, linking leading phone companies on both sides of the Atlantic.
For BT shareholders the deal is also being sugared with a promise of a special one-off 35p dividend payout and a higher rate of general dividend increases in the future.

"It is positive for BT shareholders and positive for the (telecoms) sector," said Jim McCafferty, analyst at broking house ABN AMRO Hoare Govett. For customers, the deal promises better service and lower international calling charges, while for businesses it means a company that can support them wherever they are.
The merged company will be called Concert Plc and will be the second largest international carrier after AT&T.

The deal values all of Washington, D.C.-based MCI at just over $25 billion. AS BT already owns 20 percent of MCI, it will issue Concert stock and cash worth $20.1 billion for the remaining 80 percent. Holders of MCI stock will control a third of the stock in the combined company.

Larry Stone, BT's head of EU affairs, told Reuters that he hoped the deal would be dealt with under the EU's fast-track merger rules and said he did not anticipate any anti-trust problems because the companies "operate in competitive markets".
Cable & Wireless Plc, the main British rival to BT, said that it did not expect to revive negotiations for an alliance after the merger.

"The coals on that fire are cold," C&W chief executive Richard Brown said in Singapore, referring to merger talks with BT which ended in failure six months ago. C&W is a strong player in the Asia-Pacific region, an area where BT is keen to build its presence.
Analysts now expect British Telecom and MCI to start making overtures to major Asian players such as Japan's giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp.
But while seeking an Asian partner, MCI appears to be putting another one on a backburner.

MCI is to cut its stake in a U.S. satellite television venture with media tycoon Rupert Murdoch to 20 percent from 50 percent, and has said it will probably not increase its stake in Murdoch's News Corp as originally expected.
MCI paid $1.35 billion for a stake of just under 9 percent, and could increase it to 13 percent with another $1 billion investment. ($1=.6107 Pound)
